_about: Curated table of well-established regional ENSO impacts. Each region lists the typical El Niño and La Niña rainfall/temperature signal, the season it applies to, a confidence rating, and public sources. Confidence: high = consistent across most events and models; medium = tendency, notable exceptions; low = weak or inconsistent. Boxes are [latMin, latMax, lonMin, lonMax] in degrees (lon -180..180). A place can fall in several regions; higher priority wins.

el_nino.note: Warm coastal water brings heavy rain to a normally dry coast. 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2017 brought severe floods.

citations.title: Typical El Niño Effects on Temperature and Precipitation (ENSO Cycle)
citations.quote: Wetter than normal conditions tend to be observed during December-February (DJF) along coastal Ecuador, northwestern Peru ... warmer than normal conditions during June-August along the west coast of South America.

citations.title: Typical La Niña Effects on Temperature and Precipitation (ENSO Cycle)
citations.quote: Drier than normal conditions are generally observed along coastal Ecuador, northwestern Peru and equatorial eastern Africa during DJF ... cooler than normal conditions during June-August ... along the west coast of South America.

citations.publisher: Advances in Geosciences (Copernicus), Lagos, Silva, Nickl and Mosquera 2008
citations.title: El Niño-related precipitation variability in Perú
citations.quote: El Niño in Peru is characterized by above normal sea surface temperatures (SSTs) along the coast and heavy precipitation in the northern coastal desert. The warming and rains typically begin just after Christmas ... In the extreme northern coast, seasonal precipitation begins during El Niños around November and ends around March.

citations.publisher: NOAA Climate.gov ENSO Blog (Ken Takahashi, 24 Aug 2015)
citations.title: One forecaster's view on extreme El Niño in the eastern Pacific
citations.quote: Piura, a city in the coastal desert in northern Peru, experienced annual rainfall amounts equivalent to the other 40 rainiest years combined! ... Especially in Peru, El Niño can lead to very different rainfall impacts depending on whether the warming occurs in the eastern (wetter) or central Pacific (drier).

citations.title: Heavy summer rains flood Peru
citations.quote: Water temperatures off the coast of South America, especially Peru and Ecuador, were well-above normal, exceeding 9°F in some locations. ... The Southern Hemisphere summer—December through March—is also roughly the rainy season for most of Peru—rains extend into April.

review.el_nino: agree - NOAA CPC, Climate.gov and Lagos et al. (2008) all show much-wetter conditions along coastal Ecuador and northern Peru with warm coastal SSTs in the austral summer (rains start ~Nov/Dec, peak Jan-Mar, taper in April), with the caveat that the wet signal is strongest for eastern-Pacific/coastal El Niños and can be weak or even dry for central-Pacific events.
review.la_nina: partly - CPC shows drier-than-normal DJF along coastal Ecuador/northwestern Peru, but because the coast is a desert that receives significant rain only in El Niño years the "drier" signal is essentially the absence of El Niño rains rather than a marked drought; the cooler signal on the CPC map is drawn for June-August along the west coast, not December-April.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño: keep "much wetter, warmer, Dec-Apr" but consider adding a note that the strong wet signal applies to eastern-Pacific/coastal El Niños; central-Pacific events can leave coastal Peru near-normal or drier (Climate.gov/Takahashi 2015). Temperature: CPC's typical-effects map places the warm anomaly along the west coast of South America in Jun-Aug, though coastal SSTs are also anomalously warm in Dec-Apr during coastal events. La Niña: change "drier" to "drier (already arid; mainly absence of El Niño rains)" and note that CPC's cooler-than-normal signal for the west coast is drawn for Jun-Aug rather than Dec-Apr; medium confidence is appropriate.

citations.publisher: NOAA Climate Prediction Center (1997-98 warm episode assessment)
citations.title: South America
citations.quote: During warm episodes, drier-than-normal conditions are generally observed across northeastern South America during July-March

review.el_nino: partly - the drier signal is strongly and consistently supported (CPC, WMO, Cai et al. 2020), but the fetched sources anchor it to Dec-Feb (CPC) or Jul-Mar (CPC 1997 assessment / Ropelewski & Halpert), not Dec-May, and none of the fetched pages explicitly list northern South America as warmer (CPC's DJF warm list names southeastern Brazil, not the north), so the temperature entry rests on general Amazon-drought literature rather than a quoted teleconnection page.
review.la_nina: agree - CPC's La Niña pattern page gives wetter-than-normal Dec-Feb over northern South America and lists no DJF temperature anomaly there (near normal is a fair reading), though it does add a cooler-than-normal signal for Jun-Aug across northern South America that the row omits; only one fetched authoritative source covers this phase, so medium confidence is appropriate.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño season: change "Dec-May" to "Dec-Feb (core); dry signal often begins Jul-Sep" - CPC's teleconnection page places the northern South America dry signal in DJF and the CPC 1997 assessment (following Ropelewski & Halpert 1987) gives Jul-Mar for northeastern South America; no fetched source extends the signal to May. El Niño temp: keep "warmer" but note it is not on CPC's DJF warm-anomaly list for northern South America (rain signal is the robust one). La Niña temp: change "near normal" to "near normal (Dec-Feb); cooler Jun-Aug" per CPC's La Niña page.

el_nino.note: The main rainy season often fails or comes late in strong El Niño years.

la_nina.note: Rainy season tends to be stronger.

citations.title: South America

citations.publisher: Atmósfera (UNAM), vol. 15 no. 2, 2002 – De Souza & Ambrizzi
citations.title: ENSO impacts on the South American rainfall during 1980s: Hadley and Walker circulation
citations.quote: El Niño: "caused drought conditions in the rainy seasons of the Guyana, Surinam, French Guiana, center-east of the Amazon and most of the Northeast Brazil". La Niña: "the Guyana, the Amazon and the Brazilian Northeast regions exhibit significant positive deviations of precipitation in the periods of DJF and MAM".

citations.publisher: Geophysical Research Letters (AGU), 41, 1012-1018, 2014 – Rodrigues & McPhaden (abstract retrieved via Crossref record for DOI 10.1002/2013GL058703)
citations.title: Why did the 2011–2012 La Niña cause a severe drought in the Brazilian Northeast?
citations.quote: The Brazilian Northeast (NE) is strongly affected by El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO). During La Niña events, the precipitation over the NE is generally above average. However, during the last La Niña event in 2011–2012, the NE went through its worst drought in the last 30 years.

citations.title: North-east Brazil rainfall
citations.quote: The wet season is between February and May with considerable year-to-year and decade-to-decade variability.

review.el_nino: agree (rain and season); temperature unsupported — NOAA CPC and Ropelewski & Halpert-based sources consistently show reduced rainfall in Northeast Brazil during El Niño in the JFM / DJF-MAM rainy season, but none of the fetched sources documents a warmer-than-normal temperature signal for the Nordeste specifically (CPC's warm-episode temperature composites name southeastern Brazil, not the Northeast).
review.la_nina: agree, with a documented exception — La Niña rainfall over the Nordeste is "generally above average" in DJF-MAM (De Souza & Ambrizzi 2002; Rodrigues & McPhaden 2014), but Central-Pacific-type La Niñas can flip the tropical Atlantic SST gradient and produce drought (2011-12 was the worst in 30 years), which justifies keeping confidence at medium rather than high.
review.suggested_wording_change: Rain and season wording are fine (Feb-May matches the Met Office definition of the wet season and the JFM/DJF-MAM windows in the NOAA/peer-reviewed sources; the CPC composite actually shows dryness extending Jul-Mar, so Feb-May is a conservative core). Two refinements: (1) El Niño temp "warmer" has no direct published support for the Nordeste in the fetched sources — either downgrade the temperature element to low confidence or reword to "warmer (indirect: reduced cloud/rain)"; (2) add a La Niña caveat such as "wetter (not guaranteed: Central-Pacific-type La Niñas, e.g. 2011-12, can bring drought)", since the sign of the NE rainfall anomaly depends on the tropical Atlantic SST gradient set up by the La Niña flavour.

el_nino.note: Southern Brazil, Uruguay, northeastern Argentina and Paraguay usually get heavy spring and summer rain and river floods.

la_nina.note: Drier spring and summer; crop stress is common.

citations.title: Typical Impacts of Warm (El Niño) Episodes
citations.quote: Wetter than normal conditions during warm episodes are observed along the west coast of tropical South America, and at subtropical latitudes of North America (Gulf Coast) and South America (southern Brazil to central Argentina).

citations.title: Typical Impacts of Cold (La Niña) Episodes
citations.quote: Drier than normal conditions during cold episodes are observed along the west coast of tropical South America, and at subtropical latitudes of North America (Gulf Coast) and South America (southern Brazil to central Argentina) during their respective winter seasons.

citations.publisher: Nature Reviews Earth & Environment (Cai et al. 2020)
citations.title: Climate impacts of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation on South America
citations.quote: El Niño is typically accompanied by drought in the Amazon and north-eastern SA, but flooding in the tropical west coast and south-eastern SA, with marked socio-economic effects.

citations.title: La Niña has peaked, but impacts continue (9 Feb 2021)
citations.quote: Much of this region has seen below normal rainfall over the last few months, with Uruguay, central Brazil and northern Argentina seeing significantly below normal rainfall totals.

citations.title: WMO: Prepare for El Niño (2 Jun 2026)
citations.quote: It is typically associated with increased rainfall in parts of southern South America, the southern United States, parts of the Horn of Africa and central Asia...

review.el_nino: agree - NOAA CPC, WMO and the Cai et al. 2020 review all state wetter-than-normal conditions (with flood risk) from southern Brazil to central/northeastern Argentina and Uruguay during El Niño; none of the fetched sources give a temperature signal, consistent with "near normal".
review.la_nina: partly - NOAA CPC lists drier-than-normal conditions from southern Brazil to central Argentina under La Niña and WMO documented significantly below-normal Oct-Dec 2020 rainfall in Uruguay and northern Argentina, but the CPC text frames the typical dry signal "during their respective winter seasons", so the fetched agency wording does not squarely support an Oct-Mar season for the La Niña phase.
review.suggested_wording_change: Keep rain signs and "near normal" temperature; refine season. El Niño: "wetter, strongest Oct-Dec (austral spring) and again Apr-Jun; weaker in mid-summer" - the peer-reviewed literature (Grimm, Barros & Doyle 2000 J. Climate; Cai et al. 2020) places the SESA wet peak in spring/early summer with a secondary autumn-winter response, so a flat Oct-Mar overstates Jan-Mar. La Niña: "drier, mainly Oct-Dec and winter (JJA); signal weaker and less consistent than El Niño" - the CPC page explicitly ties the La Niña dry signal to the winter season, and La Niña teleconnections to SESA are known to be weaker/asymmetric, so lower the La Niña confidence to medium unless the season is widened.

el_nino.note: Winter storms tend to be wetter.

la_nina.note: Winter rains tend to be weak.

citations.title: Climate Assessment for 1997 - South America
citations.quote: During warm episodes, drier-than-normal conditions are generally observed across northeastern South America during July-March, while enhanced precipitation tends to be observed throughout southeastern South America during November-February (Ropelewski and Halpert 1987), and throughout central Chile during the austral winter (Aceituno 1988).

citations.publisher: NOAA Climate.gov (ENSO Blog, A. Barnston, 28 May 2015)
citations.title: With El Niño likely, what climate impacts are favored for this summer?
citations.quote: Central Chile tends to be wetter than average, as does southeastern South America (e.g., eastern Argentina). [in the section 'Global El Niño Impacts during June-August']

citations.publisher: Center for Climate and Resilience Research (CR)2, Universidad de Chile (Garreaud, Aceituno, Rondanelli, Martinez-Villalobos)
citations.title: Analisis CR2 | La Nina que viene...
citations.quote: los inviernos de años El Niño tienden a presentar lluvias sobre el promedio, mientras que inviernos durante la Niña tienden a ser deficitarias.

citations.publisher: Journal of Climate 16(2), 281-296 (2003), via Universidad de Chile repository
citations.title: Montecinos & Aceituno (2003): Seasonality of the ENSO-Related Rainfall Variability in Central Chile and Associated Circulation Anomalies
citations.quote: During El Niño episodes there is a tendency for the occurrence of above-average precipitation between 30° and 35°S in winter [June-July-August (JJA)] and from 35° to 38°S in late spring [October-November (ON)], while rainfall deficit is typically observed from around 38° to 41°S during the following summer [January-February-March (JFM)] ... Opposite rainfall anomalies are characteristic during La Niña events.

citations.publisher: Direccion General de Aeronautica Civil / Direccion Meteorologica de Chile
citations.title: Fenomenos El Nino y La Nina: proyeccion otono-invierno (updated 9 Mar 2026)
citations.quote: este fenómeno suele asociarse a mayores precipitaciones en la zona centro y centro-sur durante otoño e invierno, además de temperaturas mínimas ligeramente más altas

review.el_nino: agree - NOAA CPC, Climate.gov, the Chilean met service (DMC/DGAC) and the peer-reviewed literature all state that central Chile winters (JJA, rainy season May-Oct peaking Jun-Jul) tend to be wetter than average during El Niño; the signal is one of the most robust ENSO teleconnections in South America.
review.la_nina: agree - CR2 (Garreaud/Aceituno et al.) and Montecinos & Aceituno (2003) state La Niña winters tend to have below-average rainfall in central Chile ("opposite rainfall anomalies"); the drying signal is real but somewhat less consistent than the El Niño wet signal, so medium confidence is appropriate.
review.suggested_wording_change: Rain/season wording is essentially right but could be refined: the El Niño wet / La Niña dry signal is strongest for roughly 30-35S (Coquimbo to Maule, incl. Santiago) in JJA; the rainy season runs May-Oct, so "May-Sep" or "Jun-Aug" would match the published seasons slightly better than "Jun-Sep". Note the sign reverses toward the south: from ~38-41S (Araucania/Los Rios) El Niño tends to bring drier conditions in the following summer (JFM), so the row should be scoped to central Chile north of ~38S. For temperature, DMC/DGAC notes El Niño winters tend to have slightly higher minimum temperatures (milder winters), so "near normal / slightly milder nights" is more accurate than plain "near normal" for El Niño.

el_nino.note: Summer rains tend to be weaker on the high plateau; the coast below can be wet at the same time.

citations.publisher: Center for Climate and Resilience Research (CR2), Universidad de Chile - analysis by René Garreaud
citations.title: Analysis | The Chilean Altiplano: When it rains, it pours
citations.quote: years with more prevailing easterly winds – which tend to occur during La Niña conditions – favour precipitation in the Altiplano. In contrast, in years where westerlies are more prevalent – which tends to happen with El Niño – precipitation in the Altiplano is reduced.

citations.publisher: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences (Copernicus / EGU) - Canedo-Rosso et al. 2021
citations.title: Drought impact in the Bolivian Altiplano agriculture associated with the El Niño–Southern Oscillation using satellite imagery data
citations.quote: The positive phase of ENSO is generally associated with warmer and dryer conditions, while the negative phase is associated with cooling and wetter conditions.

citations.title: The effect of El Niño on weather in the Andes
citations.quote: areas above 2,000 m receive less rain and experience higher temperatures than normal ... During La Niña years ... the opposite generally occurs

review.el_nino: agree - Garreaud (CR2), Canedo-Rosso et al. 2021 (NHESS) and GRID-Arendal all state that El Niño brings reduced summer (DJF, the ~70%-of-annual-rain monsoon season) precipitation and warmer conditions to the Altiplano via strengthened westerlies and tropospheric warming, though the literature notes that not every El Niño produces drought and the signal is strongest over the western/southern Altiplano.
review.la_nina: agree - the same sources describe La Niña as the wet phase (easterlies favour Altiplano summer rainfall) with cooler conditions; the sign is consistent across sources, but the wet response is less robust than the El Niño dry response and weakens toward the eastern Andean slopes near the Amazon.
review.suggested_wording_change: Rain/temp/season wording is supported as written (El Niño drier and warmer, La Niña wetter and cooler, Dec-Mar wet season). Suggest raising La Niña confidence from low to medium, since Garreaud (CR2) and Canedo-Rosso et al. (NHESS 2021) both state the wet/cool La Niña association explicitly. Optionally add a qualifier: "signal strongest in the western and southern Altiplano (Lake Titicaca-Poopó basin, Chilean/Bolivian plateau); weaker and less consistent on the eastern slopes; not every El Niño produces drought."

el_nino.note: Rainy season starts late and the mid-summer dry spell (canícula) is longer, especially in the Dry Corridor.

la_nina.note: More rain and a more active Atlantic hurricane season.

citations.quote: ...it is typically associated with increased rainfall in parts of southern South America, the southern United States, parts of the Horn of Africa and central Asia, and drier conditions over Central America, northern South America, the Caribbean, Australia, Indonesia, and parts of southern Asia. [...] The Central America region expects drier and warmer conditions according to the Central America Climate Outlook Forum.

citations.title: WMO steps up action on La Niña (23 December 2020)
citations.quote: Meanwhile, wetter than average conditions are forecast across Australia, especially along the east coast, where there has recently been severe flooding. The western equatorial Pacific and Central America are also more likely to see above average rainfall.

citations.publisher: Instituto Meteorológico Nacional de Costa Rica (national met service)
citations.title: ENSO - IMN
citations.quote: When the Intertropical Convergence Zone is located in the South of Central America, and over South America, under the ENSO warm phase alters rainfall in a large part of Central America, decreasing in the Pacific regions, on the other hand in the Caribbean heaviest rains occur that the climatological average.

citations.title: El Niño event likely to result in decreased rainfall in Central America and the Caribbean (9 July 2014)
citations.quote: Strong precipitation decreases relative to average typically occur during El Niño events over Central America and the Caribbean. [...] maize crops are likely to be negatively affected during the final stages of crop development due to a prolonged canícula.

review.el_nino: agree - WMO, FEWS NET and the Costa Rica IMN all describe El Niño as drier and warmer over Central America during the May-Dec rainy season (prolonged Jul-Aug canícula, weak Aug-Dec postrera), with the one refinement that the signal is strongest on the Pacific slope / Dry Corridor while the Caribbean slope of Costa Rica and Panama can be wetter than normal.
review.la_nina: partly - WMO and the Central America Climate Outlook Forum support above-normal rainfall in Central America under La Niña (the Aug-Oct 2024 LXXV FCAC outlook, issued with La Niña developing, projected above-normal rain and a weaker/wetter canícula on the Pacific, North and Central regions of Nicaragua), but the fetched WMO sentence refers to a Jan-Mar outlook, the wet signal is weaker and less consistent than the El Niño dry signal, and the Caribbean side can be drier; near-normal temperature is not contradicted (WMO's Nov 2022 release only noted raised odds of above-normal temperatures in northern Central America).
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño: keep "drier / warmer" but qualify as "drier on the Pacific slope and Dry Corridor (Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Pacific Costa Rica, southern Mexico); Caribbean slope of Costa Rica and Panama often wetter", season "May-Dec" (WMO/FAO cite Jun-Dec; a prolonged Jul-Aug canícula and a weak Aug-Dec postrera are the hallmark impacts), because IMN and FEWS NET document the opposite-sign Caribbean response. La Niña: change "wetter" to "wetter, mainly on the Pacific slope (weaker canícula, wetter Aug-Nov); signal weaker and less consistent than El Niño's and can persist into Dec-Mar", because the WMO statement supporting the wet signal covers Jan-Mar and the regional forums place the wet response on the Pacific regions rather than region-wide.

el_nino.note: Drier wet season and usually fewer Atlantic hurricanes.

citations.publisher: Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology (CIMH) / Caribbean Regional Climate Centre (WMO RCC)
citations.title: Glossary of Terms – Caribbean Regional Climate Centre
citations.quote: El Niño conditions are a major driver of regional drought in the Caribbean and can further decrease the Atlantic Hurricane Season activity. Furthermore, El Niño conditions tend to also increase temperatures in the Caribbean for several months. [...] La Niña conditions tend to increase chances of extreme rainfall in the Caribbean and can increase the Atlantic Hurricane Season activity. Furthermore, La Niña conditions tend to also slightly decrease temperatures in the Caribbean for several months.

citations.title: WMO: Prepare for El Niño (2 June 2026)
citations.quote: El Niño is typically associated with increased rainfall in parts of southern South America, the southern United States, parts of the Horn of Africa and central Asia, and drier conditions over Central America, northern South America, the Caribbean, Australia, Indonesia, and parts of southern Asia.

citations.title: Caribbean Climate Outlook Newsletter, January to March 2022 (Brief Climate Outlook April to June 2022)
citations.quote: Expected impacts on rainfall and temperatures: La Niña tilts the odds to more rainfall activity in JFM and AMJ, except in the northern Caribbean where it tilts the odds to less rainfall. [...] The ABC islands and the Windward Islands may end up drier than normal with the rest of the region predicted to be as wet or wetter than normal.

review.el_nino: agree — the regional WMO climate centre (CIMH) calls El Niño a major driver of Caribbean drought with raised temperatures for several months, and WMO lists the Caribbean among regions with drier conditions; the sources do not pin the season to Jun-Nov exactly, but the drought signal is a wet-season (roughly Jun-Oct, strongest Aug-Oct) effect, with warmth and dryness often persisting into the following dry season (Dec-Apr).
review.la_nina: partly — CIMH says La Niña raises the chance of extreme rainfall and more active hurricane seasons and slightly lowers temperatures, but CariCOF outlooks show the wetter signal is not region-wide: the northern/northwestern Caribbean (Bahamas, Cuba, Cayman), the ABC islands and sometimes the Windwards tilt drier, so "wetter" applies mainly to the central and eastern Caribbean, and "near normal" temperature is acceptable (sources say slightly cooler).
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño: keep "drier / warmer, Jun-Nov" but note that the drought signal is strongest in the late wet season (Aug-Oct) and that heat and dryness commonly persist into the following dry season (Dec-Apr); also suppressed Atlantic hurricane activity. La Niña: change "wetter" to "wetter (mainly central and eastern Caribbean); northwestern Caribbean (Cuba, Bahamas, Cayman) and ABC islands can be drier" and change temp to "near normal to slightly cooler"; add "increased extreme-rainfall and hurricane risk". Reason: CariCOF/CIMH outlooks show an opposite-sign La Niña rainfall response in the northern Caribbean and ABC islands, and CIMH describes La Niña temperatures as slightly decreased rather than unchanged.

regions.name: Southern United States and northern Mexico

el_nino.note: A stronger jet stream steers more winter storms across California, the Southwest, Texas, the Gulf coast and the Southeast.

la_nina.note: Winter tends to be dry and warm across the southern states.

citations.title: United States El Niño Impacts
citations.quote: In general, El Niño-related temperature and precipitation impacts across the United States occur during the cold half of the year (October through March). The most reliable of these signals (the one that has been observed most frequently) is wetter-than-average conditions along the Gulf Coast from Texas to Florida during this 6-month period.

citations.title: ENSO and the southwest United States "megadrought"
citations.quote: El Niño is generally associated with cooler and wetter winters in the Southwest ... La Niña is linked to drier, warmer winters over the region.

citations.title: Winner or bust? Did La Niña shape North American precipitation this winter as expected?
citations.quote: Storms are deflected toward the northern part of North America, keeping southern North America drier than average. ... most of the southern U.S. and northern Mexico were predicted to be and turned out to be drier than average

review.el_nino: agree — NOAA Climate.gov confirms wetter (and cooler) cold-season conditions across the southern tier, with the Gulf Coast Texas-to-Florida wet signal the most reliable ENSO signal in the U.S. (>80% of events), though the wet relationship is weaker and strength-dependent over California/the Southwest and the cooler-temperature signal is less robust than the rain signal.
review.la_nina: agree — NOAA Climate.gov describes the typical La Niña winter as warmer- and drier-than-average across the southern tier of the United States and drier than average across northern Mexico, driven by the northward-shifted Pacific jet stream.
review.suggested_wording_change: Season is fine but NOAA frames the El Niño impact window as October-March (cold half of the year), so "Oct-Mar" would match the source more closely than "Nov-Mar". Consider a footnote that the El Niño wet signal is strongest along the Gulf Coast (Texas to Florida) and weaker/strength-dependent over California and the Southwest, and that the "cooler" temperature signal is less reliable than the "wetter" rain signal (NOAA's national impact page does not name a southern-US temperature signal at all; only regional pages describe it as cooler). Northern Mexico evidence from NOAA is for La Niña drier; the El Niño wetter/cooler statement for northern Mexico rests on secondary sources, so confidence for the Mexico part of the row is medium rather than high.

el_nino.note: Milder, drier winters and less mountain snow.

la_nina.note: Cooler, wetter winters with more snow.

citations.publisher: NOAA National Weather Service, Spokane WA
citations.title: El Nino Pattern and Inland Northwest Snow Stats
citations.quote: El Nino winters often bring warmer than normal temperatures and below normal snowfall. These impacts are largely due to the Pacific jet steam sending low pressure systems south of the region into California, and the polar jet stream keeping cold air bottled up across eastern Canada.

citations.publisher: NOAA National Weather Service, Spokane WA
citations.title: La Nina Pattern and Inland Northwest Snow Stats
citations.quote: La Nina winters often bring cooler than normal temperatures and above normal precipitation. This combination brings above normal snowfall for an average La Nina. These impacts are largely due to blocking high pressure that builds in the Eastern Pacific, resulting in a cooler northwest flow with the storm track aimed at the Pacific Northwest.

citations.title: United States El Niño Impacts
citations.quote: there is a less-reliable dry signal in the Pacific Northwest and the northern Rockies

citations.title: La Niña in the Northwest: What can we expect?
citations.quote: In Idaho, Oregon, Washington, and most of Alaska, winter is usually cooler during La Niña events, and conditions can be wetter than normal

citations.title: ENSO Cycle: Typical North American Winter Impacts
citations.quote: milder than normal winter across the northern states and western Canada

citations.title: Weather: El Niño
citations.quote: El Niño often brings milder weather to western, northwestern and central Canada. Canada is mostly affected by El Niño during winter and spring.

review.el_nino: partly: the warmer signal is robust and consistently stated by NWS, CPC and ECCC, but Climate.gov explicitly calls the Pacific Northwest dry signal "less-reliable" and NWS/UW frame the main precipitation impact as reduced snowfall/snowpack (more rain than snow) rather than a strong deficit in total precipitation.
review.la_nina: agree: NWS Spokane and the USDA Northwest Climate Hub both state cooler-than-normal winters with above-normal precipitation and snowfall, driven by the storm track aimed at the Pacific Northwest; western Canada coverage is weaker (ECCC page fetched covers only El Niño), and USDA hedges the wet signal as "can be wetter".
review.suggested_wording_change: Keep Nov-Mar and "warmer" for El Niño, but soften "drier" to "slightly drier / less snow" (or note "warmer; reduced mountain snowpack; weak dry signal"), because Climate.gov describes the PNW dry signal as less reliable and the NWS/UW sources emphasize below-normal snowfall from warmth rather than a strong precipitation deficit. Temperature confidence for El Niño could be high while precipitation stays low; the combined row rating of medium is defensible. Climate.gov uses Oct-Mar as the impact window, so Nov-Mar is compatible.

regions.name: Northern United States and southern Canada

el_nino.note: Winters tend to be milder than usual across the northern Plains, Midwest and Great Lakes.

la_nina.note: Colder, snowier winters in the northern tier and Ohio Valley.

citations.title: ENSO Cycle: North American winter impacts of El Niño and La Niña
citations.quote: This shift results in an exceptionally stormy winter and increased precipitation across California and the southern U.S, and less stormy conditions across the northern part of the country. ... These conditions result in a milder than normal winter across the northern states and western Canada. [La Niña:] large portions of central North America experience increased storminess, increased precipitation, and an increased frequency of significant cold-air outbreaks

citations.title: How El Niño and La Niña affect the winter jet stream and U.S. climate
citations.quote: Southern and interior Alaska and the Pacific Northwest tend to be cooler and wetter than average ... the Ohio and Upper Mississippi River Valleys may be wetter than usual. ... During El Niño, these deviations from the average are approximately (but not exactly) reversed.

citations.title: Weather: El Niño
citations.quote: El Niño often brings milder weather to western, northwestern and central Canada, while eastern Canada usually experiences lesser effects.

citations.title: Get Climate Smart: El Niño
citations.quote: El Niño typically results in warmer and drier winters in northern US and Western Canada ... La Niña often brings a colder and snowier winter to western provinces, particularly British Columbia and the Prairies, and can lead to increased snowfall in parts of Ontario and Quebec

review.el_nino: partly — the "warmer, Dec-Feb" signal is strongly supported (CPC, NWS, ECCC all say milder winters across the northern states and western Canada), but the published sources describe precipitation as "less stormy"/drier over the northern tier, Pacific Northwest, northern Rockies and western/southern Canada rather than "near normal", with the dry signal weak and unreliable east of the Rockies (Great Lakes/Northeast/eastern Canada).
review.la_nina: agree — CPC describes increased storminess, increased precipitation and more frequent significant cold-air outbreaks over central North America, Climate.gov shows the Pacific Northwest cooler and wetter and the Ohio/Upper Mississippi valleys wetter, and Canadian sources describe colder, snowier winters in BC and the Prairies with more snow in parts of Ontario/Quebec; the signal is weakest in the Northeast and eastern Canada.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño rain: change "near normal" to "near normal to drier" (or "drier in the west, near normal in the east"). Reason: NOAA CPC says El Niño brings "less stormy conditions across the northern part of the country", Climate.gov notes a (less-reliable) dry signal in the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, and Canadian sources describe drier winters with less snow in western/southern Canada; the dry tendency fades toward the Great Lakes, Northeast and eastern Canada. Temperature "warmer" and season Dec-Feb are correct for both phases. La Niña wording is fine, but a note that the cool/wet signal is strongest in the Pacific Northwest, northern Rockies/Plains, Ohio Valley and western Canada and weak in the Northeast/eastern Canada would refine it.

el_nino.note: Winters are usually much warmer than normal.

citations.title: United States El Niño Impacts
citations.quote: However, winters are typically warmer than average over large parts of the state during El Nino years. ... There isn't a well defined precipitation signal over Alaska in any case.

citations.publisher: NOAA Climate.gov (ENSO Blog, B. Brettschneider, 23 Jun 2022)
citations.title: Moose tracks through Alaska and ENSO
citations.quote: La Niña winters are typically cooler than average (22 out of 28 winters), El Niño winters are typically warmer than average (20 out of 30 winters) ... there is a strong inverse relationship between ENSO and winter precipitation in Alaska

citations.title: How El Niño and La Niña affect the winter jet stream and U.S. climate
citations.quote: Southern and interior Alaska and the Pacific Northwest tend to be cooler and wetter than average [during La Niña winters].

citations.title: La Nina, El Nino and Northern Arizona Weather
citations.quote: Western Canada and Alaska along with portions of the Midwestern United States tend to enjoy a much warmer than normal winter as well. ... Western Canada and Alaska tend to experience a cooler than normal winter as well.

review.el_nino: agree — NOAA sources consistently give warmer-than-average Alaska winters under El Niño (20 of 30 winters per Brettschneider), and precipitation is either undefined (Halpert) or slightly drier (Brettschneider), so "near normal / warmer / Nov-Mar" is well supported, with winter (DJF) being the core season.
review.la_nina: partly — cooler winters are strongly supported (22 of 28 winters), but the precipitation entry is arguable: Climate.gov's jet-stream graphic and Brettschneider both describe La Niña Alaska winters as wetter, while the Halpert blog says there is no well-defined precipitation signal, so "near normal" is defensible but "slightly wetter" would match the more recent Alaska-specific analysis.
review.suggested_wording_change: Consider changing La Niña rain from "near normal" to "near normal to wetter" (Climate.gov: "Southern and interior Alaska ... tend to be cooler and wetter than average"; Brettschneider: "strong inverse relationship between ENSO and winter precipitation"), and optionally El Niño rain to "near normal to drier"; keep the precip wording hedged because Halpert states there is no well-defined precipitation signal over Alaska. Temperature signals are strongest in DJF; Nov-Mar is acceptable but note that the relationship weakens or reverses in spring and fall. La Niña temperature confidence could be raised to high (22 of 28 winters cooler).

el_nino.note: Wet season is often weak; drought risk rises in late winter and spring.

That leads to an elevated likelihood of a wet winter during La Niña ... La Niñas have brought about an additional inch of rainfall above the long-term average

citations.publisher: NOAA Pacific ENSO Applications Climate (PEAC) Center / NWS Honolulu / Pacific RISA fact sheet (2015)
citations.title: El Niño and its Impacts on The Hawaiian Islands
citations.quote: By November, a rapid decline in rainfall begins, sinking to well below average by February of the following year. The level of these dry conditions depends on the intensity of the El Niño event, though widespread dryness across the Hawai'ian Islands is typical.

citations.publisher: Journal of Climate 33(22):9929-9948 (Lu, Chu, Kim & Karamperidou 2020, doi:10.1175/JCLI-D-19-0985.1)
citations.title: Hawaiian Regional Climate Variability during Two Types of El Niño
citations.quote: As a result of this robust signal, dry conditions prevail in Hawaii ... The near-surface minimum temperature from three stations in Hawaii reveals cooling during EP winters and slight warming during CP winters.

citations.publisher: NOAA National Weather Service Honolulu (Media Advisory, 15 Oct 2021)
citations.title: Wet Season Rainfall Outlook for the State of Hawaii (October 2021 through April 2022)
citations.quote: La Nina has returned and is expected to continue into spring 2022. Climate model consensus favors above average rainfall through the wet season. Stronger La Nina events can have a higher than normal trade wind frequency which will focus rainfall on windward areas.

review.el_nino: partly: the drier Nov-Apr wet-season signal is strongly and consistently supported (NOAA Climate.gov, PEAC/NWS Honolulu, Chu 1995 lineage, Lu et al. 2020), but no fetched official source states that El Niño makes Hawaii's air temperature warmer, and Lu et al. 2020 found station minimum temperatures cool during eastern-Pacific El Niño winters (only slight warming in central-Pacific events), so "warmer" is not supported.
review.la_nina: agree, with a caveat: NOAA Climate.gov and NWS Honolulu wet-season outlooks describe an elevated likelihood of an above-average Nov-Apr wet season, but the signal is weaker than El Niño's (about +1 inch vs -3 inches at Honolulu), has weakened since 1983 (O'Connor et al. 2015 as cited in Lu et al. 2020), weak La Niña winters have had near-average rainfall (NWS Honolulu 2016), and stronger events focus rain on windward slopes while leeward areas can stay dry; "near normal" temperature is consistent with the absence of any documented temperature signal.
review.suggested_wording_change: Change El Niño temp from "warmer" to "near normal" (or "mixed/near normal"): published evidence describes El Niño impacts on Hawaii as a rainfall (drier, Nov-Apr, strongest Jan-Feb) and ocean-temperature signal, not an air-temperature warming; Lu et al. 2020 found cooler minimum temperatures in EP El Niño winters. Keep rain "drier", season "Nov-Apr" (optionally note "strongest Jan-Mar" and that the preceding Aug-Oct of a developing El Niño tends to be wetter). El Niño rain confidence can be raised to high. For La Niña, consider "wetter (weaker signal; windward-focused in strong events)" and keep season Nov-Apr at medium confidence.

regions.name: India, Pakistan, Nepal and Bangladesh (summer monsoon)

el_nino.note: The summer monsoon tends to be weaker and patchier. Not every El Niño brings drought, but the risk is clearly higher.

la_nina.note: Monsoon tends to be stronger with more floods.

citations.title: ENSO and the Indian Monsoon… not as straightforward as you'd think (Tom Di Liberto, 1 July 2014)
citations.quote: El Niño generally suppresses monsoon rainfall ... During the 14 El Niño years, summer rains ranged from well below-average to average, and even above-average. ... during the 16 La Niña years, Indian summer rains were above or around average nearly every time.

citations.title: ENSO and All-India Rainfall
citations.quote: ENSO has a profound impact on summer monsoonal rainfall across India as most major droughts are shown to occur during El Niño events. Conversely, above average rainfall is shown to occur during La Niña events.

citations.publisher: South Asian Climate Outlook Forum (SASCOF-34), WMO RCC Pune / IMD
citations.title: SASCOF-34 Consensus Outlook Statement for the 2026 Southwest Monsoon Season (June–September)
citations.quote: Below normal rainfall is most likely during the 2026 southwest monsoon season (June – September) over most parts of South Asia, particularly across the central parts of the region. ... minimum and maximum temperatures are expected to be above normal across most of South Asia.

review.el_nino: agree (partly on temperature): NOAA, IRI and the WMO-backed SASCOF-34 outlook all tie El Niño to below-normal Jun-Sep monsoon rain over South Asia, but NOAA stresses the link is imperfect (1997-98 strong El Niño gave above-average rain), SASCOF says the dry signal is strongest over the central region while north-western, north-eastern and parts of the southern region may be normal to above normal, and "warmer" rests only on the 2026 SASCOF outlook rather than a documented ENSO temperature teleconnection.
review.la_nina: agree: NOAA (above or around average in nearly all 16 La Niña years) and IRI (above-average rainfall during La Niña events) support wetter Jun-Sep conditions for India; no fetched source addressed monsoon-season temperature under La Niña, so "near normal" is unverified but not contradicted, and evidence is India-centric rather than Pakistan/Nepal/Bangladesh-specific.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño rain: "drier (strongest over central India / central South Asia; north-west Pakistan, north-east India/Bangladesh and parts of the south can be near or above normal; not every El Niño brings deficit)". El Niño temp: "warmer (low confidence; based on RCOF outlooks, not an established ENSO teleconnection)". La Niña rain: "wetter (India; weaker evidence for Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh)". Reason: SASCOF-34 documents sub-regional exceptions and NOAA documents the 1997-98 counter-example; the temperature signal is not documented as a climatological teleconnection in any fetched source.

regions.name: Sri Lanka and southern India (northeast monsoon)

el_nino.note: The October-December rains tend to be heavier.

citations.quote: During El Niño events rainfall increases for the first 3 months of the Maha season (SIM: October–December) and decreases during the last 3 months (NEM: January–March).

citations.quote: we found that Sri Lanka's winter rainfall response to El Niño/La Niña is asymmetric, with a significant response during El Niño. citations.publisher: The Morning (Sri Lanka), quoting Sri Lanka Department of Meteorology duty meteorologist Malith Fernando, 2026
citations.title: El Niño: NOAA points to Oct.–Dec. impact
citations.quote: A significant increase in rainfall may occur during October and November, followed by decreased rainfall from January to around April

review.el_nino: agree - peer-reviewed work (Sengupta & Nigam; De Silva & Hornberger; Zubair & Ropelewski 2006 cited but not fetched) and the Sri Lanka Department of Meteorology all indicate wetter Oct-Dec over Sri Lanka and southeastern peninsular India during El Niño, with the signal weak in October, strongest in November, and reversing to drier from roughly January onward; no source addressed temperature, so "near normal" is unverified but not contradicted.
review.la_nina: partly - the only fetched La Niña evidence (Kajakokulan et al. 2025) finds the La Niña rainfall response over Sri Lanka is significantly weaker than the El Niño response (asymmetric), which supports a weak/near-normal entry at low confidence; unfetched secondary sources (IMD Chennai NEM reports, Prasanna et al. 2020) suggest pure La Niña years tend toward below-normal northeast-monsoon rain over Tamil Nadu, so a slight dry lean cannot be ruled out.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño rain: keep "wetter" but note the wet signal is concentrated in Oct-Nov (second inter-monsoon; weak in October, strongest in November) and tends to flip drier from about January, so Oct-Dec is the right window and Dec-Feb should not be extended. La Niña rain: "near normal to slightly drier (weak, asymmetric signal)" rather than plain "near normal", since the La Niña response is weaker than El Niño's and secondary sources lean dry for Tamil Nadu. Temperature "near normal" for both phases is unsupported by any fetched source (no evidence either way).

citations.quote: "During the Southwest Monsoon months from June to September the correlation of ENSO with rainfall over Singapore is strong"

review.el_nino: agree - NOAA CPC, MetMalaysia, MSS/ASEAN RCC and Climate.gov all give below-average rainfall over Indonesia/Malaysia/Maritime Continent with warmer conditions following the dry spells; the drying spans the Jun-Aug dry season through the Nov-Feb northeast monsoon for Borneo and eastern Indonesia, while for Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore MetMalaysia and MSS place the reliable signal in the Jun-Sep southwest monsoon.
review.la_nina: partly - wetter is well supported (CPC, MetMalaysia, MSS, Climate.gov), but CPC's schematic places the Indonesia wet anomaly in the Dec-Feb season rather than Jun-Dec, MSS states La Niña brings the opposite of El Niño in temperature too (i.e. slightly cooler, not near normal), and the sources treat the La Niña response as the weaker, less consistent mirror of El Niño.

La Niña: "wetter, slightly cooler" (MSS: opposite conditions for rainfall and consequently temperature) with season Jun-Feb, since CPC places the wet anomaly in Dec-Feb; lower confidence to medium because the La Niña response is weaker and less consistent than El Niño's.

la_nina.note: Wetter, with more typhoons crossing the islands.

review.el_nino: agree — HKO, Wang et al. 2000 and Zhang et al. 2016 together document wetter coastal South China in the El Niño winter and spring and enhanced Yangtze summer rainfall/flooding in the decay summer, so a Dec-Aug wet signal is supported, although the post-El Niño summer response is known to vary between events (Zhang et al. 2020, Frontiers) and HKO's reprint notes El Niño years tend to be warmer rather than near normal.

review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño: keep rain "wetter" for Dec-Aug (wet winter/spring on the South China coast, wet Yangtze summer in the decay year) but consider temp "warmer" rather than "near normal" for the winter half, since HKO reports El Niño onset/following years tend to be warmer on the whole. La Niña: extend the cooler season to Sep-Feb (HKO cites a stronger northeast monsoon in both autumn and winter) and soften rain to "drier (weak/inconsistent)" because published work shows La Niña winters since ~1980 have often been cold and wet in southern China; low confidence is appropriate.
