review.la_nina: partly: the strengthened-winter-monsoon cold tendency is documented by JMA (2008) and the Ma & Chen review, but with "smaller amplitudes" than El Niño, and JMA's current Dec-Feb statistics show no statistically significant temperature or precipitation tendency for any region of Japan; the cold signal is also strongest in southern East Asia and in the first winter of a La Niña event.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño rain: change "near normal" to "near normal; wetter on Pacific side of Japan, Okinawa and Korea" (JMA winter statistics show above-normal precipitation on the Pacific side of eastern Japan and Okinawa/Amami; KMA reports warmer and wetter winters). El Niño temp: keep "warmer" but note the signal is modest (JMA: "normal or warmer" in western Japan, strongest in the first half of winter and weaker when El Niño onsets late). La Niña temp: keep "cooler" but qualify as "slightly cooler / weak and inconsistent" because JMA finds no statistically significant Dec-Feb temperature or precipitation tendency in Japan, the review describes La Niña effects as of smaller amplitude than El Niño, and JMA's global map places the cold tendency over southern rather than northern East Asia. Season Dec-Feb is correct for both phases.

regions.name: Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands and Vanuatu

el_nino.note: Long dry spells; highland frost and crop loss in PNG in 1997 and 2015.

la_nina.note: Wetter, with cyclones more likely to the west.

citations.publisher: Pacific-Australia Climate Change Science and Adaptation Planning Program (Australian Bureau of Meteorology / CSIRO) with Papua New Guinea National Weather Service
citations.title: Current and future climate of Papua New Guinea (2015)
citations.quote: Generally in Papua New Guinea El Niño years are usually drier than normal while La Niña events are usually wetter. [...] The dry season at Port Moresby is cooler than normal in El Niño years and warmer than normal in La Niña years, while the wet season tends to be warmer and drier than normal during an El Niño event.

citations.publisher: Vanuatu Meteorology and Geo-hazards Department with PACCSAP (Australian Bureau of Meteorology / CSIRO)
citations.title: Current and future climate of Vanuatu (2015)
citations.quote: In both Port Vila and Aneityum El Niño events tend to bring drier conditions as well as a late start to the wet season and cooler than normal dry seasons. The opposite occurs during La Niña events.

citations.publisher: Pacific Climate Change Science Program (Australian Bureau of Meteorology / CSIRO) with Solomon Islands Meteorological Service
citations.title: Climate Change in the Pacific, Volume 2: Country Reports, Chapter 13: Solomon Islands (2011)
citations.quote: El Niño events tend to bring drier conditions in the wet season through a delayed onset of the WPM, often until late January or February, and a weaker or displaced SPCZ and ITCZ. [...] During La Niña years wet season rainfall is usually above normal and temperatures are usually lower.

review.el_nino: partly: all three national/PACCSAP sources confirm El Niño is clearly drier (delayed monsoon onset, droughts) across PNG, Solomon Islands and Vanuatu, but the temperature sign is season-dependent - warmer only in the wet season (Nov-Apr), while the dry season (May-Oct) is explicitly cooler than normal in all three countries, so a blanket "warmer" over a Jun-Feb window is wrong for roughly half that window.
review.la_nina: agree (with refinement): sources say La Niña years are usually wetter (PNG, Solomon Islands wet season, Vanuatu "the opposite"), with flooding and landslides; temperature is mixed rather than strictly near normal - cooler wet season (Solomon Islands) but warmer dry season (PNG, Vanuatu), which nets out to roughly "near normal" over a multi-season window.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño temp: change "warmer" to "warmer in wet season (Nov-Apr), cooler in dry season (May-Oct)" or simply "mixed" - PNG, Vanuatu and Solomon Islands sources all state El Niño dry seasons are cooler than normal (cooler surrounding ocean, reduced cloud only in wet season), and only wet-season temperatures are above normal. La Niña temp: "near normal" is acceptable but "cooler wet season, warmer dry season" is more faithful. Season: keep Jun-Feb for the rain impact if the intent is the drought window (dry season plus delayed monsoon onset "often until late January or February"), but note the statistically significant rainfall signal at Honiara/Santa Cruz is confined to the wet season (Nov-Apr); dry-season rainfall correlations with ENSO are not significant there, and only dry-season maximum temperature responds.

regions.name: Kiribati, Tuvalu, Nauru and the Marshall Islands

el_nino.note: Rain moves toward the central Pacific; equatorial atolls become much wetter, with higher sea levels in some areas.

citations.publisher: Australian Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO (Pacific Climate Change Science Program)
citations.title: Current and future climate of Kiribati
citations.quote: Across Kiribati, El Niño events tend to bring wetter, warmer conditions than normal. [...] Droughts can be very severe in Kiribati, and are usually associated with La Niña events. [...] The wet season usually lasts from around November to April.

citations.publisher: Australian Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO (Pacific Climate Change Science Program)
citations.title: Current and future climate of Tuvalu
citations.quote: In Funafuti, El Niño events tend to bring wetter, warmer conditions than normal, while La Niña events usually bring drier, cooler than normal conditions. [...] a wet season from November to April and a dry season from May to October

citations.publisher: Australian Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO (Pacific Climate Change Science Program)
citations.title: Current and future climate of Nauru
citations.quote: In Nauru, El Niño events tend to bring warmer, wetter conditions than normal, while La Niña events are associated with a delayed onset of the wet season and drier than normal conditions, often resulting in an extended drought.

citations.publisher: NOAA Pacific ENSO Applications Climate (PEAC) Center / Pacific RISA
citations.title: El Niño and its Impacts on the Republic of the Marshall Islands
citations.quote: El Niño poses the threat of major drought for the RMI. Rainfall during El Niño is greater than average during the first half of the year. After September, the monthly rainfall begins a steady decline, sinking to well below average during the first few months (January through May) of the year following El Niño.

review.el_nino: partly: the "much wetter, warmer" signal is well documented for Kiribati, Tuvalu and Nauru (BoM/CSIRO country profiles), but for the Marshall Islands PEAC shows the opposite sign within the row's Oct-Apr window, with rainfall declining after September and falling well below average from January to May of the year after El Niño, often producing severe drought.
review.la_nina: agree: BoM/CSIRO profiles for Kiribati, Tuvalu and Nauru all tie La Niña to drier-than-normal conditions and severe or extended drought (Nauru also a delayed wet-season onset); the Tuvalu profile describes La Niña as cooler than normal rather than near normal, and the Marshall Islands are generally reported as near-normal rainfall under La Niña (PEAC bulletins, not fetched here), so the "much drier" label is strongest for the three equatorial nations.
review.suggested_wording_change: Season: change "Oct-Apr" to "Nov-Apr" (BoM/CSIRO give the wet season as November to April for Tarawa and Funafuti; note Kiritimati's wet season is Jan-Jun, so eastern Kiribati peaks later). El Niño: keep "much wetter, warmer" for Kiribati, Tuvalu and Nauru but footnote or split out the Marshall Islands, where rain is above average only in the first half of the El Niño year and drops well below average Jan-May of the following year (PEAC), i.e. drought rather than wet during the row's season; El Niño confidence can return to "high" if RMI is separated. La Niña temp: "near normal to slightly cooler" (Tuvalu profile says cooler than normal). La Niña rain: "much drier" holds for Kiribati/Tuvalu/Nauru; RMI is closer to near-normal.

regions.name: Fiji, Tonga, Samoa, Cook Islands and New Caledonia

el_nino.note: The main rain band shifts northeast, so Fiji, Tonga and New Caledonia tend to be drier. Cyclones can reach farther east than usual.

citations.title: Fiji Climate Outlook, March 2026 (Vol. 20, Issue 3) - El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) section
citations.quote: El Niño events usually result in reduction of Fiji's rainfall. [...] It is the suppression of rainfall during the Cool/Dry Season (May to October) that is normally of most concern. [...] Usually La Niña results in wetter than normal conditions for Fiji, occasionally leading to flooding during the Warm/Wet Season (November to April).

citations.publisher: Cook Islands Meteorological Service / Pacific Climate Change Science Program (BoM-CSIRO)
citations.title: Climate, climate variability and change of Cook Islands
citations.quote: During La Niña events rainfall increases during the wet season (November to April), when the SPCZ lies northwest to southeast over the island group. During El Niño years the SPCZ moves more to the northeast of the Southern Cooks causing lower than normal rainfall, drought like conditions and stronger south-east trade winds.

citations.publisher: Australian Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO, Pacific Climate Change Science Program
citations.title: Climate Change in the Pacific: Scientific Assessment and New Research, Volume 2: Country Reports, Chapter 5: Fiji Islands (section 5.5 Climate Variability)
citations.quote: In the wet season the impact of ENSO is very strong. In El Niño years Nadi Airport wet seasons are drier [...] and days are warmer. Much of this variability is driven by the SPCZ, which moves to the north-east, away from Fiji, during El Niño events. [...] The opposite changes tend to occur in La Niña years.

citations.title: El Niño : quels impacts pour la Nouvelle-Calédonie ? (19 June 2026)
citations.quote: une diminution des précipitations entre septembre et avril (de l'ordre de – 20 % en moyenne) [...] des températures plus basses (– 0,5 °C en moyenne) entre mai et janvier, pendant la phase montante d'El Niño

citations.publisher: Pacific RISA / NOAA (East-West Center, University of Hawaii)
citations.title: El Niño and its Impacts on American Samoa (2015 fact sheet)
citations.quote: Rainfall during the year of a strong El Niño starts out below normal in August and dryness continues through June of the year after El Niño. [...] With weak and moderate El Niño's rainfall can be above normal, however this response is not consistent.

review.el_nino: agree - Fiji Met Service, Cook Islands Met Service, Météo-France NC, Tonga Met Service (via PINA, 22 Jun 2026) and the BoM/CSIRO PCCSP Fiji chapter all state El Niño brings below-normal rainfall via a north-eastward SPCZ shift, though the dry signal begins in the preceding May-Oct dry season (Fiji says that is the season of most concern) and the Samoa response is weaker/inconsistent for weak-moderate events.
review.la_nina: agree - Fiji Met Service ("wetter than normal ... flooding during the Warm/Wet Season (November to April)") and Cook Islands Met Service ("rainfall increases during the wet season (November to April)") directly support wetter Nov-Apr; the PCCSP Fiji chapter says the opposite of the El Niño changes occurs in La Niña years; no fetched source gives a Samoa- or Tonga-specific La Niña statement.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño season: widen to "May-Apr (dry-season onset May-Oct through wet season Nov-Apr)" or add a note that the drying starts in the May-Oct dry season - Fiji Met Service says dry-season rainfall suppression is "normally of most concern" and Météo-France NC gives Sep-Apr (about -20%); Nov-Apr alone understates the exposure. El Niño temp: "near normal" is a simplification - PCCSP Fiji reports warmer days in the wet season at Nadi and cooler, drier dry seasons, and Météo-France NC reports about -0.5 °C during the El Niño ramp-up (May-Jan); consider "mixed: cooler nights/dry season, warmer days in wet season" or keep "near normal" with low confidence on temp. Regional caveat: the Samoa signal is weaker and inconsistent for weak-moderate El Niño (Pacific RISA fact sheet), because Samoa sits near the SPCZ pivot; consider flagging Samoa as lower confidence. La Niña Nov-Apr wetter is supported as written.

el_nino.note: Winter and spring rain is usually well below normal, with more heatwaves and bushfire risk; the northern wet season starts later.

la_nina.note: Wetter, with more floods and more tropical cyclones.

citations.title: What is El Niño and what might it mean for Australia?
citations.quote: The shift in rainfall away from the western Pacific, associated with El Niño, means that Australian rainfall is usually reduced through winter–spring, particularly across the eastern and northern parts of the continent. Nine of the ten driest winter–spring periods on record for eastern Australia occurred during El Niño years.

citations.title: What is La Niña and how does it impact Australia?
citations.quote: The increased rainfall and cloudiness in the western Pacific associated with La Niña usually means above-average winter–spring rainfall for Australia, particularly across the east and north. ... Unlike El Niño years, the impacts of La Niña often continue into the warm months.

citations.publisher: NOAA Climate.gov (ENSO Blog, Andrew Watkins, 24 Sep 2015)
citations.title: El Niño from the other side of the Pacific pond
citations.quote: in Australia, it often brings the exact opposite: a dry winter and spring in the east, coupled with unusually warm to hot weather.

citations.title: El Niño and La Niña (Climate knowledge centre)
citations.quote: The greatest impact on Australia's weather is in winter and spring – and for La Niña, into summer.

review.el_nino: partly: drier and warmer for eastern/northern Australia is well supported, but BOM places the signal in winter–spring (Jun–Nov) and states the rainfall influence "typically reduces around early summer", so the Jun–Feb season is too long; also BOM notes warmer daytime maxima are strongest in southern Australia while winter–spring nights are often cooler (more frost) in the east, and northern-tropics rainfall is only reduced in the early wet season.
review.la_nina: agree: BOM documents above-average winter–spring rainfall across the east and north that, unlike El Niño, continues into summer (Dec–Mar rainfall in eastern Australia ~20% above average), with cooler daytime maxima south of the tropics; the one refinement is that overnight minima tend to be warmer across northern and eastern Australia, so "cooler" applies to daytime temperatures.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño season should be "Jun-Nov" (winter–spring), not Jun-Feb: BOM says Australian rainfall is reduced "through winter–spring" and "the influence on Australia's rainfall patterns typically reduces around early summer"; consider temp wording "warmer days" (nights can be cooler/frostier in winter–spring in the east). La Niña Jun-Feb is fine (BOM: impacts "continue into the warm months"; Dec–Mar eastern rainfall 20% above average); consider "cooler days" since minima are warmer in the north and east.

el_nino.note: Signal is weaker than in the east.

citations.title: What is El Niño and how does it impact Australia? (issued June 2014, updated March 2021)
citations.quote: Australian rainfall is usually reduced through winter–spring, particularly across the eastern and northern parts of the continent. ... El Niño years tend to see warmer-than-average temperatures across most of southern Australia, particularly during the second half of the year.

citations.title: What is La Niña and how does it impact Australia? (issued August 2016)
citations.quote: La Niña usually means above-average winter–spring rainfall for Australia, particularly across the east and north. ... La Niña years tend to see cooler than average maximum temperatures across most of mainland Australia south of the tropics, particularly during the second half of the year.

citations.publisher: Geophysical Research Letters (AGU/Wiley), van Rensch, McGregor & Gallant, 31 Dec 2025 (Vol. 53, Issue 1)
citations.title: The Extent of El Niño and La Niña Influence on Australian Rainfall
citations.quote: The reduction of rainfall during El Niño is comparatively limited; confined mainly to El Niño's developing phase and the southeast and northeast of Australia. ... El Niño can suppress rainfall for up to 5 months in localized coastal regions of northern and southwest Australia. ... A reduced chance of rainfall during El Niño is only expected in about 3–4 months of the year in winter-spring

citations.publisher: Water Corporation (Western Australia state water utility)
citations.title: What is El Niño and how does it affect WA?
citations.quote: When El Niño occurs alongside a positive IOD or positive SAM, warmer and drier conditions become more likely, particularly across southern Western Australia.

review.el_nino: partly - BOM confirms warmer-than-average conditions across most of southern Australia in the second half of the year and reduced winter-spring rainfall, but BOM and van Rensch et al. (2026) both place the rainfall reduction mainly in eastern/northern and southeastern Australia, with only localized coastal drying in southwest WA; the Water Corporation notes the SW-WA drying signal becomes likely mainly when El Niño coincides with a positive IOD or positive SAM.
review.la_nina: partly - "near normal" rain is defensible for southwest WA because BOM's above-average winter-spring rainfall statement is qualified to the east and north (and van Rensch shows La Niña wetting mainly eastern/northern Australia), but "near normal" temperature is contradicted by BOM, which states La Niña brings cooler-than-average maximum temperatures across most of mainland Australia south of the tropics in the second half of the year.
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño: rain "slightly drier (weak/localized in SW WA; clearer for southern SA/Vic; stronger when a positive IOD or SAM coincides)", temp "warmer days (spring emphasis)", season Jun-Nov OK; keep rain confidence low but temperature signal is better supported (BOM: warmer across most of southern Australia in second half of year). La Niña: rain "near normal to slightly wetter" is fine, but change temp from "near normal" to "cooler days" (BOM: cooler-than-average maximum temperatures across most of mainland Australia south of the tropics, particularly second half of year), season Jun-Nov OK. Consider splitting "southwestern" from "southern" Australia: the ENSO rainfall signal is much clearer for southern SA/Victoria than for southwest WA, where winter rainfall is driven mainly by SAM and the subtropical ridge.

el_nino.note: Stronger westerly winds: drier in the northeast, wetter in the southwest, cooler overall.

la_nina.note: More northeasterly winds bring rain to the north and east.

citations.title: The impact of El Niño and La Niña on New Zealand's climate
citations.quote: In summer, stronger or more frequent winds from the west... drier-than-normal conditions in east coast areas and more rain than normal in the west. In winter, colder southerly winds tend to prevail. [La Niña:] More north-easterly winds are characteristic, which tend to bring moist, rainy conditions to the north-east of the North Island, and reduced rainfall to the south and south-west of the South Island.

citations.title: El Niño maps and charts
citations.quote: Summer rainfall during previous El Niño events was lower than normal across large parts of New Zealand, but especially in the north and east of both islands.

citations.title: El Niño and La Niña
citations.quote: Aotearoa New Zealand typically experiences more westerlies during El Niño... This leads to wetter and cooler conditions in the west of the country but drier and warmer conditions in the east. [La Niña:] more frequent northeasterly winds... bringing more rainfall to the northeast of the North Island. Temperatures are generally warmer than normal around the country.

review.el_nino: partly - the drier north-and-east rain signal in summer is well supported (NIWA, MetService), but "cooler" is a winter/west-of-country signal: NIWA ties cooling to winter southerlies, and MetService and NIWA's 2026 outlook say the east is typically warmer/drier in summer (Salinger in The Conversation: cooler overall, although eastern areas can still experience warmer than average summers).
review.la_nina: agree - NIWA and MetService both give more north-easterlies with wetter conditions in the north-east of the North Island, reduced rainfall in the south/south-west of the South Island, and generally warmer-than-normal temperatures; neither source ties the signal specifically to Dec-Feb (described as a general/year-round tendency).
review.suggested_wording_change: El Niño temp: change "cooler" to "cooler in the west/south, but warmer and drier in the east" (or "mixed: cooler overall, east often warmer"), because NIWA attributes the national cooling to winter southerlies while summer brings westerlies that make the east drier and warmer (MetService; NIWA El Niño 2026 outlook notes eastern spikes in high temperatures). El Niño rain: keep "drier (north and east)" but optionally add "wetter west/Southland" since the western side is wetter. La Niña rain: refine "wetter (north and east)" to "wetter (north-east of North Island); drier south/south-west of South Island" per NIWA and MetService. Both phases: consider noting that NIWA states ENSO explains less than 25 percent of year-to-year variance in seasonal rainfall and temperature at most NZ locations, which justifies medium rather than high confidence; the Dec-Feb season is directly supported for El Niño rain but La Niña is described as a general tendency rather than a summer-specific one.

regions.name: Kenya, Somalia, southern Ethiopia, Uganda and northern Tanzania

el_nino.note: The October-December short rains are usually heavy, with flooding along rivers and in low areas. 1997 and 2023 saw severe floods.

la_nina.note: Short rains fail more often; repeated La Niña years led to the 2020-23 Horn of Africa drought.

citations.title: Climate Assessment for 1997 - Africa (Equatorial Eastern Africa)
citations.quote: The year-to-year variability of rainfall during the OND season shows a strong relationship to the ENSO (Ropelewski and Halpert 1987, 1989), with above-normal rainfall observed during Pacific warm episodes and below-normal rainfall observed during Pacific cold episodes.

citations.publisher: ICPAC (IGAD Climate Prediction and Applications Centre, WMO Regional Climate Centre)
citations.title: El Niño Southern Oscillation and Indian Ocean Dipole Watch for the Eastern Africa short rains season (October-December 2023)
citations.quote: El Niño is frequently associated with enhanced rainfall in the eastern part of Eastern Africa during the OND season. ... During the La Niña phase of ENSO when the SSTs are reversed, suppressed rainfall is often observed in the equatorial parts of the region, as experienced in OND 2020, 2021, and 2022.

citations.title: November El Niño update: It's a small world
citations.quote: El Niño tends to enhance the 'short rains' rainy season (the 'long rains' season, which is much less ENSO-sensitive, is March-May), leading to wetter conditions.

review.el_nino: agree — NOAA CPC, Climate.gov and ICPAC all state El Niño enhances the Oct-Dec short rains (record 5-10x normal in OND 1997), though ICPAC stresses the signal is strongest in the eastern part of the region and can fail when the Indian Ocean Dipole is unfavourable (e.g. OND 2018 was below average despite El Niño).
review.la_nina: agree — CPC states below-normal OND rainfall during Pacific cold episodes and ICPAC documents suppressed OND rainfall in the equatorial parts of the region in La Niña years 2020, 2021 and 2022 (and forecast the same for 2024), with the strongest impact in Somalia, southern Ethiopia and the arid/semi-arid lands of Kenya.
review.suggested_wording_change: Keep season Oct-Dec and signs, but qualify the region: El Niño rain 'wetter, often much wetter in eastern Kenya, Somalia and southern Ethiopia; weaker and less consistent in Uganda and northern Tanzania' — ICPAC restricts the strong signal to the eastern part of Eastern Africa and CPC's statement is for equatorial eastern Africa, and ICPAC notes El Niño does not always deliver above-normal rains (OND 2018 was below average) because the Indian Ocean Dipole strongly modulates the outcome. La Niña 'drier' is well supported for Somalia, southern Ethiopia and eastern Kenya; consider 'drier (strongest in Somalia, southern Ethiopia and eastern Kenya)'. Temperature: none of the fetched sources gives an ENSO temperature signal for this season, so 'near normal' is unverified rather than contradicted; consider lowering temp confidence or marking as 'no clear signal'.

regions.name: Ethiopian highlands, Eritrea and Sudan (summer rains)

el_nino.note: The main kiremt rains tend to be weaker; 2015 brought a severe drought in Ethiopia.

citations.title: Understanding El Niño and La Niña: Implications for the IGAD Region (29 June 2025)
citations.quote: During the June to September (JJAS) season, which is significant over the western and northern parts of IGAD, El Nino is known to cause depressed seasonal rainfall. [...] La Niña...often results in...enhanced rainfall during the JJAS season and northern parts of the GHA region.

citations.publisher: ICPAC / Food Security and Nutrition Working Group
citations.title: FSNWG Special Report on El Niño (August 2026)
citations.quote: In the western parts of the region, where El Niño is associated with below-average rainfall during the June-September season, parts of central and northern Ethiopia, the pastoral belt of Sudan, most of Eritrea and Djibouti...

citations.title: East Africa Seasonal Monitor, July 2026: Deepening concerns across East Africa following severe June rainfall deficits and forecast below-average July–September rains
citations.quote: El Niño conditions typically suppress the June–September rains in western and northern areas of East Africa.

citations.publisher: NOAA Institutional Repository (Cai et al., peer-reviewed review, Nature Reviews Earth & Environment)
citations.title: Climate Impacts of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation in Africa
citations.quote: During El Niño, the Somali Jet onset tends to be later and the intensity is weaker such that many drought years over the Ethiopian plateau coincide with an El Niño. [...] spatially coherent dry conditions occur from Senegal to Ethiopia accompanied by anomalously high air temperatures in sub-Saharan Africa.

review.el_nino: agree — IGAD, ICPAC, FEWS NET and the Cai et al. review all state El Niño suppresses the June-September (Kiremt/Karan) rains over northern/central Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, and the review adds anomalously high temperatures with the drying, so "drier, warmer, Jun-Sep" is supported.
review.la_nina: partly — IGAD states La Niña "often results in enhanced rainfall during the JJAS season" over the northern Greater Horn, supporting "wetter", but only one fetched source addresses it and none speaks to temperature, so the "near normal" temperature entry is unverified rather than contradicted.
review.suggested_wording_change: Season and signs are fine; refine the region note: El Niño drying is strongest over central, northern and northeastern Ethiopia, the Rift Valley, Eritrea and Sudan's pastoral belt, and weaker/less consistent in the western and southwestern highlands (ICPAC FSNWG 2026; FEWS NET 2026). Cai et al. also note the El Niño signal can be offset in some years by Atlantic SST/Saharan heat-low modulation, so "drier" should read as a tendency, not a certainty. La Niña temperature "near normal" has no published support found; consider "no clear signal".

el_nino.note: Summer rains are usually below normal with hot spells; maize harvests failed widely in 1992, 2016 and 2024.

citations.title: El Niño Temperature and Precipitation Patterns
citations.quote: Drier than normal conditions generally observed over northern South America, Central America and southern Africa during DJF ... warmer than normal conditions during December-February across southeastern Asia, southeastern Africa, Japan, southern Alaska and western/central Canada

citations.title: La Niña Patterns
citations.quote: wetter than normal conditions tend to be observed during December-February (DJF) over northern South America and southern Africa ... below-normal temperatures during December-February over southeastern Africa, Japan, southern Alaska and western/central Canada, and southeastern Brazil

citations.title: El Niño / La Niña Phenomena
citations.quote: drought conditions in eastern and northern Australia, Indonesia, southern Africa, and parts of South Asia due to suppressed monsoon activity

citations.title: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation teleconnection to southern Africa in a changing climate
citations.quote: El Niño (La Niña) events in southern Africa characterized by dry (wet) conditions during the austral summer

review.el_nino: agree: NOAA CPC, WMO and Steinkopf & Engelbrecht (2025) all describe drier and warmer-than-normal austral summer (DJF) conditions over southern/southeastern Africa during El Niño.
review.la_nina: partly: rainfall "wetter" in DJF is well supported (CPC, ERL 2025), but CPC's composite gives below-normal (cooler) DJF temperatures over southeastern Africa rather than "near normal".
review.suggested_wording_change: La Niña temp: change "near normal" to "cooler" (NOAA CPC La Niña composite lists below-normal DJF temperatures over southeastern Africa; SAWS also describes La Niña summers as cooler and wetter). Season: sources anchor the signal to DJF (austral summer); "Dec-Mar" is acceptable but "Dec-Feb" matches the published composites more exactly. Optionally note that the signal is strongest over the summer-rainfall region (roughly south of 15°S, especially eastern South Africa/Zimbabwe/Mozambique/Botswana) and that the winter-rainfall Western Cape does not follow this pattern.

el_nino.note: The south and west tend to be drier; cyclone activity shifts.

citations.title: El Niño and Rainfall (ENSO teleconnection map, 2023; based on Mason & Goddard 2001 and Lenssen, Goddard & Mason 2020)
citations.quote: El Niño conditions in the tropical Pacific are known to shift rainfall patterns in many different parts of the world. The regions and seasons shown on the map below indicate typical but not guaranteed impacts of El Niño. [Map: 'Dry' region labelled 'Nov-Mar' covers southern Africa and the southern half of Madagascar; northern Madagascar is unshaded.]

citations.title: La Niña and Rainfall (ENSO teleconnection map, 2023)
citations.quote: La Niña conditions in the tropical Pacific are known to shift rainfall patterns in many different parts of the world. The regions and seasons shown on the map below indicate typical but not guaranteed impacts of La Niña. [Map: 'Wet' region labelled 'Nov-Apr' covers southern Africa and the southern/south-western third of Madagascar only.]

citations.publisher: NOAA Institutional Repository (accepted manuscript of Cai et al., Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, 2025)
citations.title: Climate Impacts of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation in Africa
citations.quote: During El Niño, southern Africa (south of ~15oS) experiences warmer and drier conditions in austral summer (Fig. 2c) (Supplementary Fig. 2c) as low-level moisture convergence and cloud band development are suppressed. [...] During La Niña, the impact reverses. [...] leading to colder and wetter conditions south of ~15oS.

citations.publisher: World Weather Attribution (Harrington et al., 2021; co-authored with Madagascar Direction Générale de la Météorologie)
citations.title: Attribution of severe low rainfall in southern Madagascar, 2019-21
citations.quote: a statistically significant relationship between ENSO and seasonal rainfall was found over both Southern Africa and Eastern Africa, with El Niño events aligning with low- and high-rainfall anomalies, respectively (see Figure 10 below). However, the strength of this correlation was less significant over southern Madagascar

review.el_nino: agree (partly on season): IRI's map shows a typical Nov-Mar dry signal over southern Madagascar (not the north) and Cai et al. 2025 give warmer and drier austral-summer conditions south of ~15°S, but WWA (Harrington et al. 2021) finds the ENSO-rainfall correlation weaker over southern Madagascar than over mainland southern Africa and notes the strong 1997/98 El Niño brought a normal rainy season there.
review.la_nina: partly: IRI's La Niña map shows a Nov-Apr wet signal reaching only the southern/south-western third of Madagascar and Cai et al. 2025 describe colder and wetter conditions south of ~15°S, but WWA documents an extremely dry 2020/21 summer in southern Madagascar during a moderate La Niña, so the signal is weak and regionally limited; "near normal" temperature is defensible though the review says cooler.
review.suggested_wording_change: Season: change both phases from "Dec-Mar" to "Nov-Mar" (El Niño) and "Nov-Apr" (La Niña) to match the IRI teleconnection maps. La Niña rain: change "wetter" to "wetter (south and west)" because the IRI wet region covers only the southern/south-western third of the island, and northern Madagascar shows no signal in either phase. Optionally La Niña temp "near normal to slightly cooler" (Cai et al. 2025: "colder and wetter conditions south of ~15°S"), keeping confidence low given the dry 2020/21 La Niña summer in the Grand Sud.

review.el_nino: agree - Peer-reviewed work on the Nov-Apr cold season (Hoell et al. 2017; Mariotti 2007) finds El Niño persistently linked to wetter conditions over Iraq, Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan, though the signal is strongest in the autumn and spring transition months and has strengthened since the 1980s; the "near normal" temperature entry is not addressed by any source I could load.

review.suggested_wording_change: Keep rain: "wetter" (El Niño) / "drier" (La Niña) and season "Nov-Apr", but add a note that the signal is strongest in the autumn (Oct-Dec) and spring (Mar-Apr) shoulders of the season rather than midwinter (Mariotti 2007), and that the La Niña drying is less consistent than El Niño wetting (Hoell et al. 2017: El Niño wet throughout 1901-2012, La Niña dry only since the 1970s).
